---
title: "Work with project data"
---

You now have a working **`[DX]` notebook** running with R.

In this section, you will use R to read a small synthetic dataset stored in your DNAnexus project, inspect it, create a simple summary table, and produce a figure.

All of the code needed for these exercises is already included in your `getting-started.ipynb` notebook.

::: {.callout-important title="This tutorial uses synthetic data"}
The file used on this page contains **synthetic training data only**. It does not contain information from MCPS participants.

If you are completing this tutorial from a real MCPS research project, you do **not** need to access the real research data.
:::

## 1. Find the training data

The shared training dataset is stored in:

```text
mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/
└── data/
    └── example_data.csv
```

This file is stored persistently in your DNAnexus project.

When R is running inside JupyterLab, project files are available under:

```text
/mnt/project/
```

So the full path used by R is:

```text
/mnt/project/mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/data/example_data.csv
```

::: {.callout-note title="Remember `/mnt/project/`"}
For this tutorial, you can think of `/mnt/project/` as meaning **"files stored in my current DNAnexus project".**

The paths you need are already provided in the notebook. You do not need to memorise or type them yourself.
:::


::: {.callout-note title="For larger or more complex analyses"}
Reading directly from `/mnt/project/` works well when you need to **read a file once**, as we do in this tutorial.

For larger or more complex analyses — particularly when the same files need to be accessed repeatedly — it may be more efficient to first make a **temporary copy of the required files in the JupyterLab computing environment** and work from that copy.

We will not need to do this in this tutorial. The important point for now is that `/mnt/project/` gives R direct, read-only access to files stored in your DNAnexus project.
:::

## 2. Read the data into R

In `getting-started.ipynb`, find the section **2. Read the training data** and run the supplied code:

```r
dat <- read.csv(
  "/mnt/project/mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/data/example_data.csv"
)

head(dat)
```

The first command reads the persistent CSV file into R and creates an object called `dat`.

The second command displays the first few rows.

You should see variables including `id`, `age`, `sex`, `height_cm`, `weight_kg`, and `systolic_bp`.

The identifiers begin with `TRAINING` to make it clear that these are not real MCPS participant identifiers.

## 3. Project file versus R object

There are now two related but different things:

| Item | Where it is | Persistent? |
|---|---|---|
| `example_data.csv` | DNAnexus project | **Yes** |
| `dat` | Current R session | **No** |

The original CSV remains stored in the project.

`dat` is an R object created in the temporary computing environment so that you can analyse the data.

::: {.callout-tip title="The code connects the two"}
Your notebook contains the instruction needed to recreate `dat`:

```r
dat <- read.csv(
  "/mnt/project/mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/data/example_data.csv"
)
```

If you start a new R session later, you can simply run this code again.
:::

## 4. Inspect the data

Find the section **3. Inspect the data**.

First run:

```r
dim(dat)
```

This reports the number of rows and columns in the dataset.

Then run:

```r
summary(dat)
```

This produces a basic summary of each variable.

The purpose here is not to learn these R functions in detail. It is simply to confirm that R can work normally with data stored in your DNAnexus project.

## 5. Create a summary table

Find **4. Create a simple summary table** and run:

```r
aggregate(age ~ sex, data = dat, FUN = mean)
```

This calculates the mean age for each value of `sex`.

The resulting table appears directly below the code cell in your notebook.

::: {.callout-note title="Notebook outputs can be preserved"}
Outputs displayed in your `[DX]` notebook — including tables, printed results, and model summaries — can be saved with the notebook.

This makes the notebook a useful record of both your code and the results it produced.
:::

## 6. Create a figure

Find **5. Create a figure** and run the supplied code:

```r
plot(
  dat$age,
  dat$systolic_bp,
  xlab = "Age (years)",
  ylab = "Systolic blood pressure",
  main = "Synthetic training data"
)
```

A scatter plot should appear directly below the code cell.

Again, the purpose is not the analysis itself. We are checking that your JupyterLab environment can:

1. access data stored in DNAnexus;
2. analyse the data using R; and
3. display the resulting output inside your persistent notebook.

## 7. Save your progress

Save your `[DX]` notebook now.

At this point it should contain:

- the supplied R code;
- the first rows of the synthetic dataset;
- the output from `dim()` and `summary()`;
- your summary table; and
- your figure.

We will look more closely at what is preserved when you save a `[DX]` notebook on the next page.

::: {.callout-caution title="Can't find a recently added project file?"}
The files available to R under `/mnt/project/` reflect the project files available when your JupyterLab environment was started.

If files are added to or reorganised in the DNAnexus project **after JupyterLab has started**, they may appear in the DNAnexus project browser but may not yet be available to R under `/mnt/project/`.

Restarting JupyterLab refreshes the project files available to the environment. Because restarting takes time, it is best to make sure the files you need are in the project **before starting JupyterLab**.
:::

## Checkpoint

Before continuing, confirm that:

- `example_data.csv` was read successfully from `/mnt/project/`;
- the object `dat` exists in your current R session;
- you can see the first rows of the dataset;
- the summary commands ran successfully;
- the summary table is visible;
- the figure is visible; and
- you saved your `[DX]` notebook.
